ch19.title: Gethsemane
ch19.b002: Even after the farewell discourse was over, they did not leave the upper room. The Master sat among them without ceremony and talked over what had happened to each of them along the way, and to the companies of people they had gathered. He is really going. For the first time it began to feel like a fact and not just words. Their hopes clutched at his promise to be with them again after a little while. He would go to the Father for a short visit, they thought, and then come back to set up the kingdom. Many of them understood it that way.
ch19.b003: At last the Master quieted them and began his final counsel. He was leaving them his peace, he said — not measured out as the world gives, but given in full, as much as each of them could receive. When they scattered and left the Son of Man in the hands of his enemies, they too would know something of his loneliness; but he was never alone, for the Father was always with him. In the world they would have tribulation, but they were to take heart.
ch19.b004: Then the Master rose and began to go around the table. He stopped in front of each man in turn and gave him a word of farewell and a blessing. The apostles stayed in the places where they had first reclined, and each one stood up when the Master came and spoke to him.
ch19.b005: The first was John, at his right. The Master told him he was the youngest of the brethren. He had been looking after the Master’s earthly family in his place, and he asked him to go on doing so. In these last hours John was to stay close, so that the Master could leave with him any message for his family. He had chosen John for this, he said, because he was the youngest and would likely outlive the others.
ch19.b006: John stood with both hands braced on the edge of the table. *The youngest.* For three years he had hated that word: being the youngest, having to stand behind the older men. And now, for that very reason, the Master was entrusting his mother to him.
ch19.b007: Once, the Master said, he had called John and his brother sons of thunder. John had changed a great deal since the day he wanted fire called down from heaven on the heads of thoughtless men, but he must change still more. He was to become the apostle of the new commandment given that night, and spend his life teaching his brethren to love one another as the Master had loved them.
ch19.b008: Tears ran down John’s cheeks. He looked into the Master’s face and said that he would. But how, he asked, could he learn to love his brethren more? Only a few hours earlier, coming into this room, he had been the one who moved first to claim the place at the right. He knew it. The Master told him he would love his brethren more when he first learned to love their Father in heaven more, and when he truly came to care how they fared in time and in eternity. He must live at peace with all men, and he must never quarrel with the souls he was trying to win.
ch19.b009: The Master passed around his own seat to the left and stopped beside the empty couch. He said nothing. A deep sorrow came into his face. Judas had still not come back. Even so, not one of them supposed that their treasurer had gone out to betray the Master — except, perhaps, Andrew. Too much had happened that night all at once. The warning that one of them would betray him had slipped, for the moment, out of their minds.
ch19.b010: The Man Who Would Not Falter
ch19.b011: James Zebedee sat silent, waiting for his turn. His brethren called his frequent silences his unaccountable silences. But tonight’s silence had a reason. He had seen his younger brother John weeping. He had seen the Master’s mother entrusted not to him, the elder, but to his brother. Strangely, he was not hurt. Only a foreboding pressed on his chest, a sense that some other work was set aside for him alone.
ch19.b012: The Master stood before Simon Zelotes, and Simon rose. The Master told him he was a true son of Abraham — but what a time he had had trying to make him a son of the kingdom of heaven! He knew Simon loved him and loved the kingdom, yet Simon still wanted the kingdom to come in the shape he himself desired. And the Master said he was troubled about what would happen to Simon when he was gone.
ch19.b013: Simon wiped his eyes and answered. The Master need have no fear for his loyalty; he had turned his back on everything to give his life to building the Master’s kingdom on earth, and he would not falter. He had come through every disappointment so far, and he would never forsake him.
ch19.b014: The Master put a hand on his shoulder. It was truly refreshing, he said, to hear him speak like that at such a time — but his good friend still did not understand what he was saying. Simon would not hesitate to go into battle and die for him; neither would any of the others. At that they all nodded hard. James nodded too. But that would not be asked of Simon, the Master said. And he asked him: when the Master was gone, and Simon finally woke up to the fact that he had misunderstood his teaching, what would he do then?
ch19.b015: Simon tried to say more, but the Master raised a hand and stopped him. None of the apostles was more sincere and honest at heart than Simon, he said; but none would be more shaken and downcast after he had gone. And when Simon finally saw it all and went out to preach the gospel with great power, he must never forget that the Master had been with him all through that season of discouragement. He would always be the Master’s apostle. And once more the Master warned him that those who fight with the sword perish by the sword, while those who labor in the spirit gain life everlasting.
ch19.b016: James looked at Simon’s face. Simon had his teeth clenched. The jaw of the man who had just vowed he would never falter was trembling.
ch19.b017: Next was Matthew Levi, seated beside Simon. The Master told him he would no longer need to provide for the treasury of the apostles. Very soon they would all be scattered, and none of them would have even one brother to lean on. Each of them would have to go out alone, to the ends of the earth. When Matthew asked whether Andrew would show them the way, the Master said that Andrew would remain their friend and counselor, but once the new teacher came, the Spirit of Truth would lead each of them. And then he said: Levi, you have won the trust and affection of your brethren. They all love you.
ch19.b018: Ten heads nodded together. Simon Zelotes, at Matthew’s side, nodded too — Simon, who along with Judas had been the slowest of them all to accept a publican in their company. Simon’s elbow was resting against Matthew’s arm. He did not move it away.
ch19.b019: The Master went on. Matthew’s brethren did not know it, he said, but he himself knew a great deal about Matthew’s anxieties, sacrifices, and labors to keep the treasury full.
ch19.b020: Matthew caught his breath. *I know.* For more than three years he had been waiting for those two words. The money he had quietly taken from his own purse and given in other men’s names; the replies he had swallowed under disdainful looks. This man had known all of it. From the beginning. The others heard the words as praise for the trouble he had taken collecting offerings. No one asked what the sacrifice had been. Matthew did not tell them. There was no need now. It was enough that one person knew. And that one person knew.
ch19.b021: The Master told him to let all the world see what the Father could do for a hated tax collector, and to show with his whole life that God is no respecter of persons. And he said he had loved him from the first, just as he loved these other Galileans. Matthew could not answer. It was all he could do to stay on his feet.
ch19.b022: Then the Master stood before James, and James rose. The Master reminded him of the time when he and his younger brother had come asking for places of honor in the kingdom. The Master had told them such honors were the Father’s to give, and had asked whether they were able to drink his cup. Both had said they were. They had not been able then, and perhaps were not able even now, he said, but what they were about to pass through would soon prepare them for that service.
ch19.b023: As he listened, James felt his heart give one heavy beat. *My cup.* He had said it lightly back then. He had meant that he was ready for whatever risks a revolt might bring. All he knew now was that this cup was nothing of the kind.
ch19.b024: Whether his ministry was long or short, the Master told him, he must possess his soul in patience. He and his brother would go different ways, and one of them might sit down with the Master in the eternal kingdom long before the other. He should learn that true wisdom holds discretion as well as courage, and should yoke good sense to his fiery temper. As far as it lay in his power, he should live long and bear much fruit.
ch19.b025: James looked at his brother. John was looking back at him. *Long before the other.* Which one would it be? He did not ask. Not asking was his way. But as he sat down he folded the words away deep in his chest.
ch19.b026: To the End of the Table
ch19.b027: The Master went to Andrew’s place at the end of the table. He looked this faithful helper in the eyes and told him he had represented him faithfully as head of the ambassadors. He had sometimes doubted, and at other times had been dangerously timid, but in dealing with his fellows he had always been just and fair. And now, the Master said, he was releasing him from all responsibility for governing the apostolic group. Yet being released from that office did not lessen in the least his duty to hold his brethren together, with a firm and loving hand, through the trying time just ahead. Even if the great works that men notice were not his to do, he should be content to be the teacher and counselor of those who did them.
ch19.b028: Andrew bowed his head. His face showed nothing. But James saw it. *The teacher of those who do great works.* As those words fell, Andrew’s eyes went, for just an instant, to his brother Peter at the far end of the table.
ch19.b029: The Master stood between the Alpheus twins. My little children, he called them. Hard times were coming, and even if they could not understand all that would happen, they must never doubt that they had once been called to the work of the kingdom. When this was over, they should go back gladly to their old labor; for one who knows God there is no such thing as common work, and for them, who had worked with him, everything had become sacred. They had been his apostles, and they always would be.
ch19.b030: The twins stood side by side and listened. They did not know what lay ahead. But at the words about going back to their former work, the two of them felt relief at the same moment. Work, at least, they understood.
ch19.b031: To Philip the Master said that he had asked a great many foolish questions. And then he told Philip what he had been asking himself all the while the Master was coming around the table toward him: What on earth will I do if the Master goes away and leaves us alone in the world? Philip’s face went red. Those had been his very words. He had been a good steward, the Master said, and since he had always wanted to be shown, he would very soon see great things. The world was full of people who looked at life just as he did, and he was to lead them toward the eyes of faith. And he must always remember that whoever had seen the Master had seen the Father.
ch19.b032: When the Master reached Nathaniel, Nathaniel began to rise. The Master told him to stay seated and sat down beside him — the only time in all his circuit of the table that he sat. He told Nathaniel that his unfailing sincerity had been a blessing to his fellows, but that sincerity is most useful when it is wedded to discretion.
ch19.b033: There and then Nathaniel made a frank confession. He had been listening to the Master’s teaching since the day he was first called, he said, but honestly he could not grasp its full meaning; he did not know what to expect next. He thought most of his brethren were just as puzzled. No one contradicted him. The Master laid a hand on his shoulder and said it was no wonder he was perplexed, trying to make sense of the gospel through the mold of old tradition. What he had not been able to get from the Master’s teaching and life he must now learn from the master of all teachers: actual experience. And then he told them all not to lose heart because they could not lay hold of the full meaning of the gospel.
ch19.b034: To Thomas the Master said that although he had often lacked faith, he had never once lacked courage. His brethren would come to value his critical way of weighing new teachings all the more. And his doubts, the Master said, had perplexed his brethren, but they had never troubled him. He had confidence in Thomas, and he would go before him even to the ends of the earth. Thomas took the words with his two hands clasped tight on his knees. His doubts had never troubled the Master. And they were the very thing that had troubled Thomas most of all.
ch19.b036: Last of all the Master went to Simon Peter at the lowest place. Peter stood up. James watched the two of them from across the table. The lowest place — the couch Peter had flung himself onto in anger at the start of the evening. Now it had become the place where the Master came last and lingered.
ch19.b037: The Master told Peter he knew that he loved him, and that he would give his life to proclaiming the gospel to Jew and gentile. But it grieved him that their years of close companionship had not taught Peter to think before he spoke. What would Peter have to go through, he asked, before he learned to set a guard upon his lips? That weakness did not lessen the Master’s love for him in the least. But Peter would certainly gain great help from what he would pass through this very night.
ch19.b038: Then the Master turned to them all and said that what he was saying to Peter he was saying to every one of them. This night they would all be in great danger of stumbling because of him. He reminded them of the old word that when the shepherd is struck, the sheep are scattered. But he promised that he would come back to them for a little while, and that he would go before them into Galilee.
ch19.b039: Peter put his hand on the Master’s shoulder. His whole body was shaking. Even if all his brethren gave way to doubts, he said, he would not stumble, no matter what. He would go with the Master, and if need be, he would die for him.
ch19.b040: He meant it. James knew that. No one in the room doubted it. Tears were streaming from Peter’s eyes. They were tears brimming over with love.
ch19.b041: The Master looked straight into those wet eyes. And he told him that this very night, before the cock crowed, Peter would deny him three or four times. What he had failed to learn in their peaceful days together, he would learn through much trouble and sorrow. And once he had truly learned that lesson, he was to strengthen his brethren and go on living a life given to preaching the gospel — even if that road led to prison, even to paying the highest price that love can pay.
ch19.b042: Peter opened his mouth, but nothing came out. Deny him? He? Tonight? He shook his head. It was not that he could not believe it. It was that such a thing could not be. His hand was still on the Master’s shoulder.
ch19.b043: The Master looked around at them all again and said that this very night he would ask the Father to strengthen each one of them for what they were about to go through. He loved them all with the love with which the Father loved him; and so from now on they must love one another.
ch19.b044: They sang a hymn. Then they went down the stairs and set out for the camp on the Mount of Olives.
ch19.b046: A full fifteen minutes later, torches appeared in the lane outside the house of Elijah Mark.
ch19.b047: Judas Iscariot stood in front of the temple guards and looked up at the gate. The window of the upper room was dark. After rushing out from the supper he had gone straight to his cousin’s house, and the two of them had gone together to the captain of the temple guards. He had asked the captain to gather his men; he himself would lead them to Jesus. But he had arrived earlier than expected, and it had taken time to assemble them. In the meantime the room had emptied.
ch19.b048: Judas was thrown into confusion. He had counted on the Master still being in that room. He had reckoned, too, that only two men had left the camp that afternoon wearing swords, Peter and Simon Zelotes. In the narrow lanes of a sleeping city there would be little resistance. And now his reckoning had gone wrong.
ch19.b049: The camp was another matter. There were more than sixty disciples there. He knew also that Simon Zelotes had a good store of weapons. And there were the eleven. If they found out — if they came after him — a cold sweat ran down Judas’s spine. He was not only disloyal. Deep in his heart he was a coward.
ch19.b050: He told the captain they must go back to the temple. The rulers were already gathering at the high priest’s house. Judas told them they had missed Jesus. They would have to go to Gethsemane, he said, where more than sixty followers were camped with him, all armed. And he asked for forty armed soldiers. It was the boldest thing he could bring himself to do — and that boldness was born of fear.
ch19.b051: The rulers had no such force. For more than an hour they went from one authority to the next, until at last they came to Pilate himself. The governor was reluctant to be involved, and his wife begged him not to grant the request; but since the presiding officer of the Sanhedrin had come in person to ask, he finally gave them Roman soldiers.
ch19.b052: While he waited, Judas reckoned again. A different reckoning this time. When forty soldiers stood before him, the man would surely do something at last — fire from heaven, soldiers thrown to the ground. And if in the end he would not use his power, then he had never been meant to be a king in the first place. Either way, Judas would be right. He held that thought up in front of his chest like a shield. The tremor he had felt in the upper room as he took the dipped bread still lingered in his fingertips. He rubbed his hand on the hem of his robe.
ch19.b053: At about half past eleven Judas set out from the temple. More than sixty men went with him: temple guards, Roman soldiers, and servants of the chief priests who had tagged along out of curiosity. The torches swayed as they climbed along the Kidron valley.
ch19.b055: Earlier than that, at about ten o’clock, the Master and the eleven had left the Mark house. They went through the city and crossed the brook Kidron. John Mark, wakened by the sound of them coming down the stairs, threw on nothing but a linen coat and followed.
ch19.b056: As they walked, the apostles began for the first time to talk about Judas. The words about one of them betraying the Master came back to them now. But it was not until they reached the camp and saw that Judas was not there to meet them that they spoke of him aloud. They all crowded around Andrew and asked what had become of Judas. Andrew said only that he did not know where Judas was, but he feared he had deserted them.
ch19.b057: Soon after they reached the camp, the Master said they should draw apart by themselves and pray to the Father. He led them a little further up Olivet to a place where Jerusalem lay in full view. There was a large flat rock there. He told them to kneel on it in a circle around him — as they had on the day of their ordination.
ch19.b058: James knelt. The rock was cold, and the cold soaked into his knees. He remembered the grass of that day: the chill of the winter earth, the highland looking out over the sea, the hands laid one by one upon their heads. That day there had been twelve. Tonight one place in the circle was empty. It was the place of the man on whose head the Master’s hands had rested first.
ch19.b059: The Master stood in their midst and lifted his eyes to heaven. The soft moonlight lay on his face and his garments. He told the Father that his hour had come; all that remained was to lay down his life in the flesh. He had made the Father known to these men whom the Father had chosen out of the world and given him, and they had believed. He was praying not for the world, he said, but for these men who would represent him in the world after he was gone.
ch19.b060: And he said that the Father had given him twelve men, and he had kept them all — except one, the son of revenge, who would no longer have fellowship with them.
ch19.b061: No one in the circle moved. But beside him James felt someone’s breath stop short, as if cut off. It was Simon Zelotes. That one sentence opened all their eyes. Now they knew. Now they knew what that empty place meant.
ch19.b062: The prayer went on. These men were weak and frail, but they could be trusted; he had proved them. He did not ask that the Father take them out of the world, only that he keep them from its evil. And he prayed not only for these eleven but for all who would come to believe through their word: that they might all be one, as the Father and he were one.
ch19.b063: James closed his eyes and listened to that voice. It was the tenderest voice he had ever heard, and the loneliest. He was not praying for himself. He was praying for the men he was about to leave behind — men already left short by one of their own.
ch19.b064: After the prayer ended they stayed on their knees for several minutes. Then, without a word, they went back down to the camp.
ch19.b065: Back at the camp, the fact that Judas was really gone fell on them with full weight. While the eleven were pouring out heated words about their traitorous comrade, David Zebedee and John Mark took the Master aside. They had been watching Judas for several days, they told him, and they knew he meant to hand the Master over to his enemies. The Master heard them out and said only that nothing could happen to the Son of Man unless the Father in heaven willed it.
ch19.b066: The brightness that had been in his face all evening was slowly ebbing away. The apostles were so agitated that they did not want to go to their tents. The Master told them to rest for the work of tomorrow, and that he was leaving them his peace. And as he sent them to their tents, he called Peter, James, and John to stay with him for a little while.
ch19.b067: Before the others lay down, Simon Zelotes led them to his tent. He brought out the swords and other weapons he had stored there and handed them around one by one. They all took them. All except Nathaniel. Had not the Master told them many times, Nathaniel said, that his kingdom was not of this world, and that his disciples must not fight with the sword to bring it about? They had all seen his mighty power; if he wished, he could defend himself. If he would not resist, then that must be his way of doing the Father’s will. Nathaniel would pray, but he would not wield a sword.
ch19.b068: When Andrew heard Nathaniel, he handed his sword back to Simon. He said nothing. That night nine of them lay down to sleep with swords at their sides.
ch19.b069: The apostles scattered in silence, without so much as a good night. Before Andrew went to his tent the Master held him back and told him to keep the brethren together until he came to them again, after he had drunk this cup. He was to strengthen them.
ch19.b070: None of the apostles expected anything to happen that night. Only David Zebedee and John Mark knew that Judas would bring the enemy that very night. As David went off to keep watch on the upper trail, he said good-bye to the Master, and the Master told him that he had not forgotten: others had done what they were directed to do, but David had served him from his own heart.
ch19.b072: When the camp had grown still, the Master took Peter, James, and John a short way up a nearby ravine. It was a place where he had often gone to pray. Moonlight filtered through the branches of the olive trees. The three could feel that he was crushed by something heavy. They had never seen him so weighed down.
ch19.b073: He asked them to sit there and keep watch with him. Then he went off about a stone’s throw and fell on his face to the ground.
ch19.b074: James leaned his back against the trunk of an olive tree. The words he had heard in the upper room a few hours earlier were still in his ears. *Are you able to drink my cup?* And he was the man who had said yes. He opened his eyes and looked toward the place where the Master lay. In the moonlight a pale edge of cloak lay pressed against the earth. A low voice came to him, broken by the wind. *Father.* The rest he could not hear. Ever since they had come to Jerusalem he had been short of sleep. His eyelids were as heavy as stones. He fought the weight. And he lost.
ch19.b075: A hand was shaking his shoulder. James opened his eyes. The Master was standing over them. What, he asked — could they not watch with him even for one hour? Did they not see that his soul was sorrowful even to death, and that he longed for their company? James could not answer. He looked at the Master’s face. On the moon-wet forehead stood great drops of sweat. The night was chilly. And yet the sweat was running down his face.
ch19.b076: The Master went off again and lay down. The three looked at one another. This time, James told himself, clenching his teeth, he would stay awake. A wind went through the olive leaves and turned them over. It sounded like the sea of Galilee at night. Listening to it, he sank back into sleep. While they slept, a mighty angel came down from heaven and stood beside the Master. The angel touched him and strengthened him. The three saw none of it.
ch19.b077: The Master came back and woke them again. At such an hour, he said, he needed them to watch and pray with him; they above all needed to pray that they not enter into temptation. Why did they fall asleep the moment he left them? And a third time he went apart to pray.
ch19.b078: James heard the end of that third prayer. Or rather, later he thought he had. If this cup could not pass, he would drink it; not his own will, but the Father’s be done. And a line before that, too: the Father could see his sleeping apostles; let him have mercy on them; the spirit was willing, but the flesh was weak. Whether that line had been a dream or waking, James was never able to tell. He only remembered, all his life, that it had not blamed him.
ch19.b079: When the Master came back again, they were asleep once more. He looked down at them for a long time. Then, with a gesture of pity, he told them to sleep on now and take their rest; the time of decision was past, and the hour had come when the Son of Man would be handed over to his enemies. Then he bent and shook them awake. Get up, he said; let us go back to the camp. The one who was betraying him was near, and the hour had come for his flock to be scattered.
ch19.b080: James jumped to his feet. The Master’s face was different now. The sweat had dried. The face they had always known — the calm face — had come back. James did not know where that calm had come from. All he knew was that it had not come from him. He had not been able to stay awake for even an hour. He, the man who had said he could drink the cup.
ch19.b082: The three were wide awake now. Just then two breathless messengers ran into the camp asking for David Zebedee. Peter told them where he was keeping watch, and they ran off toward him. The sentinel the Greeks had posted beside their own tents roused his countrymen, and soon the whole camp was awake — all but the eight apostles, who were sound asleep.
ch19.b083: Peter started off to wake the eight. The Master firmly forbade him. Then he gently told everyone to go back to their tents. No one obeyed. When he could not send them away, the Master left them and walked alone down toward the olive press near the entrance to Gethsemane Park. He had drawn apart on purpose, so that his captors could take him alone — so that his apostles would not see Judas betray him, fight the soldiers, and be taken and killed with him.
ch19.b084: John watched the Master’s back moving away. His feet would not move. The Master sat down alone on the broad stone of the olive press. The moonlight shone on him. The only one who saw him there was John Mark, hidden in a little shed beside the press.
ch19.b085: Some time later a line of torches and lanterns swung around the shoulder of the hill. Peter, James, and John, and the thirty or so who were camped with them, saw it. No one needed to ask whom they had come for. They all rushed down toward the olive press. The soldiers came from one side, the disciples from the other. The two groups stopped short, with the Master sitting alone in the moonlight between them.
ch19.b086: At the head of the armed band was Judas Iscariot.
ch19.b087: Judas had put himself in front on purpose. He had to get there ahead of the soldiers. He meant it to look as though he had run ahead to warn them. He would identify the man with a kiss, and then slip quickly away.
ch19.b088: Before he could reach him, the Master rose and stepped a little to one side. He asked the foremost soldier on the left, the captain of the Romans, whom they were looking for. Jesus of Nazareth, came the answer. The Master walked up and stood directly in front of the captain. And he said: I am he.
ch19.b089: His voice was not loud. Yet the soldiers in the front rank fell back and stumbled to the ground. John saw a torch drop and roll in the dirt.
ch19.b090: Now there was no need for Judas to do anything. The Master had made himself known. But Judas had to be seen keeping his bargain with the rulers. Only then could he collect the reward and the honors that had been promised. While the soldiers pulled their broken ranks together, the apostles and disciples drew nearer. Judas stepped forward.
ch19.b091: He embraced the Master and kissed him on the brow. And he greeted him: Hail, Master and Teacher. It was a greeting he had spoken countless times in more than three years.
ch19.b092: The Master called him friend. Was it not enough to do this, he asked — would he betray the Son of Man even with a kiss?
ch19.b093: John could not breathe. *Friend.* Even now the Master called him that. There was no anger in his voice. To John that was more terrible than any shout. Judas’s face was caught in the torchlight — half of it in the light, half in shadow. John never forgot that face as long as he lived.
ch19.b094: Judas froze where he stood. The pretense that he had come to warn them shattered at that one word. His mind went blank, and he did not even think of running.
ch19.b095: No one moved. At last the Master drew himself out of Judas’s embrace and went toward the soldiers. Again he asked whom they were looking for. Again the captain said, Jesus of Nazareth. The Master said he had already told them he was the one; if it was he they wanted, they should let these others go. He was ready to go with them.
ch19.b096: The Roman captain was willing enough to let the others go. But while they waited for his order, Malchus, the high priest’s Syrian bodyguard, came up and began to tie the Master’s hands behind his back — though the captain had given no such order. When Peter and the men around him saw it, they could hold back no longer. Peter drew his sword. The others drew theirs too and rushed at Malchus.
ch19.b097: Before the soldiers could step in to protect the high priest’s servant, the Master raised his hand against Peter. Sternly he told him to put his sword back. Those who take the sword perish by the sword. Did Peter not understand that it was the Father’s will that he drink this cup? Did he not know that even now he could call on more than twelve legions of angels to free him from these few men?
ch19.b098: The point of Peter’s sword trembled. Then it went down.
ch19.b099: The Master had stopped the resistance, but it was enough to frighten the captain of the guards. He had his men seize the Master roughly and bind his hands with heavy cords. As the cords tightened on his wrists, the Master asked them why they had come out against him with swords and clubs, as if to catch a robber. Day after day he had taught openly in the temple, and they had not laid a hand on him.
ch19.b100: John looked at those hands. A few hours earlier they had washed his feet with the water of the basin. Now they were being lashed behind his back with coarse rope.
ch19.b101: Afraid that the Master’s followers would try to take him back, the captain of the guards ordered them seized as well. But the disciples overheard the order and moved first. They scattered and fled up into the ravine. John Mark, slipping out of the shed, was spotted by a soldier coming back from the chase. The soldier grabbed his linen coat; the boy wriggled out of it and fled naked into the dark.
ch19.b103: In his flight James Zebedee lost sight of Peter and John. He wandered among the olive trees and came back at last to the olive press. The other apostles were gathered there. John Mark had run to David with the news, and the two of them had hurried to the tents and woken the eight sleepers. The eight stood there, still half-dazed with sleep, swords in their hands. While they slept, it had all been finished.
ch19.b104: Meanwhile Peter and John, who had hidden among the olive trees, were following the band that was leading the Master away. John kept close behind the crowd. Peter followed at a distance.
ch19.b105: By the olive press a brief debate began. Andrew did not speak. He was no longer their chief; a few hours earlier the Master had released him from that burden, and he kept to it. Simon Zelotes climbed onto the stone wall of the olive press. He cried out for loyalty to the Master and the kingdom. They must go after the mob and rescue him, he said. Most of them were swept along by his fierce voice.
ch19.b106: When Simon had finished, Nathaniel stood up. He reminded them of the Master’s teaching about nonresistance, given so many times. And had not the Master told them that very night to preserve their lives for the day when they would go out and preach the gospel?
ch19.b107: James spoke up for Nathaniel. He told them what he had seen with his own eyes: when Peter and the others drew their swords, the Master had told them to put them away; he had said that those who take the sword perish by it. As he spoke, James felt the weight of the sword at his own side. When Simon was shouting, his blood had boiled too. But the Master’s face, as they bound his hands, had not asked to be rescued.
ch19.b108: Matthew and Philip spoke as well. But the debate reached no conclusion. Then Thomas spoke. He reminded them how the Master had warned Lazarus not to throw his life away. The Master would not let his friends defend him, and he refused to use his divine power against his enemies. So they could not save him, Thomas said. He urged them all to scatter, each man to look out for himself. David Zebedee would stay at the camp and keep it as a center for sending and receiving news.
ch19.b109: By half past two in the morning the camp was empty. Only David remained, with three or four messengers. Five of them — Nathaniel, Matthew, Philip, and the two Alpheus brothers — went to hide at Bethpage and Bethany. Thomas, Andrew, James, and Simon Zelotes slipped into the city to hide. The shepherd had been struck, and the sheep were scattered. Dimly they all knew that the Master had told them beforehand of this very thing. But the shock of his sudden disappearance left none of them able to think clearly.
ch19.b110: On the dark road down into the city, James thought about his brother. Where was John? He would have followed the crowd. The youngest had followed closest, and he, the elder, was going off to hide.
ch19.b111: Earlier, John had been in the midst of the band as it left the garden. At the entrance to the garden the captain of the temple guards and the Roman captain argued. The captain of the guards wanted the prisoner taken to Caiaphas; the Roman captain wanted him taken to Annas, the former high priest. The Roman had his way. Judas walked beside the two captains, but neither of them said a word to him. They despised him utterly.
ch19.b112: John remembered that the Master had told him to stay close. He hurried forward until he was at the Master’s side, where he walked between the two captains. The captain of the temple guards saw him and told his assistant to seize and bind him; he was one of this fellow’s followers. But the Roman captain looked around, saw John, and told him to come and walk by him. No one was to touch him. This man, said the Roman, was neither a traitor nor a coward; he had seen him in the garden, and he had not drawn a sword. He had the courage to come forward and be with his Master. Roman law allowed a prisoner at least one friend to stand by him.
ch19.b113: John walked beside the Roman. His legs were shaking. Courage? He knew how his feet had refused to move back by the olive press. He was close to the Master only because the Master had told him to stay close. But that was enough. That night, for the first time, he walked at the Master’s side not because he was the youngest, but for one reason only: to be there.
ch19.b114: Judas heard. *Neither a traitor nor a coward.* The words were about John, but to his ears they were aimed at him. Unable to bear the shame, he dropped back from the procession. And he walked on alone to the palace of Annas.
ch19.b115: All the way from the garden to the palace of Annas the Master did not say a single word. He walked with his hands bound. John walked beside that silence. When he glanced back, he could see a figure following far behind in the darkness — at a distance, coming no nearer and falling no farther behind. John knew who it was. It was Peter.
ch19.b117: The events follow Papers 181–183: the final admonitions and the gift of peace in the upper room (181:0.1–1.10); the personal farewell to each apostle (181:2.1–2.31, in the order John, the empty place of Judas, Simon Zelotes, Matthew, James Zebedee, Andrew, the twins, Philip, Nathaniel and all, Thomas, Peter), including Peter’s vow and the foretelling of his denial; the departure at ten o’clock, John Mark following, and Andrew’s words about Judas (182:0.1–0.3); the farewell prayer on the flat rock (182:1.1–1.7); the report of David and John Mark, the handing out of swords and Nathaniel’s refusal, the nine who went armed to bed, and the words to Andrew and David (182:2.1–2.13); the threefold prayer in Gethsemane, the sleeping apostles, and the angel (182:3.1–3.11); the olive press and the Greek sentinel (183:0.1–0.5); Judas missing Jesus at the Mark home and asking for soldiers (183:2.1–2.4); the arrest, the kiss, Peter’s sword, and John Mark’s escape (183:3.1–3.10); the debate at the olive press and the scattering (183:4.1–4.3); and the dispute of the two captains, the protection of John, Judas falling behind, and the silence of Jesus (183:5.1–5.5).
ch19.b118: Character details come from Paper 139 and related passages: James’s unaccountable silences, his fiery temper, and his being the first of the apostles to die a martyr (139:3); John as the youngest, and the one apostle who followed close behind Jesus on the night of the arrest (139:4.5, 139:4.10); Matthew secretly making up the funds without the apostles ever knowing (139:7.8–7.9); Simon Zelotes and Judas being slowest to accept the publican (139:7.3); Judas’s cowardice and his hope that Jesus would use his power (139:12.12, 183:2.2); and Jesus laying his hands first on Judas at the ordination (140:2.1).
ch19.b119: Added fiction includes the apostles’ inner thoughts and memories; sensory details such as moonlight and the sound of olive leaves; Simon’s elbow resting against Matthew’s arm; Andrew’s glance toward Peter; James believing he half heard the third prayer in a dream; Judas’s thoughts while waiting at the temple; and Judas’s face lit on one side by torchlight. The words James thinks he heard are the text’s own prayer (182:3.4); since the text does not say he actually heard it, it is left as something between dream and waking.
ch19.b120: The words of Jesus are retold, not quoted, following the sense of the text.
